presented studies. Experimental data from different BFB and CFB gasifiers have
been collected from the literature and used to evaluate the model performance,
with the aim to test whether the models are also valid for experimental
conditions other than those for which they were originally validated.” [17]
“The cases with input parameters in different ranges than those of the original
validated experiments have been chosen for the evaluation step.” [17]
“Basically each model has been validated with exactly the same data used by the
authors that developed that model. However due to further use of the input data

CHAPTER 6
CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
In previous chapters we showed that the black box model features better accuracy
in predicting four major components of product gas (H2, CH4, CO, and CO2) in a larger
range of operating conditions and captures the physics of the phenomenon with regard to
two of the most influential parameters of the process (i.e. gas yield and CCE).
● Main conclusion is that artificial neural network is a valuable and effective
tool in capturing the physics of gasification process due to a more efficient
way of quantifying interdependencies between various parameters.
● The ANN model developed in this study had significantly better accuracy
compared to other leading models.
This was accomplished through:
● Considering more experimental data as suggested by other modelers,
(building a diverse database of gasification process featuring about 40
different types of biomass and the largest range of influential parameters
compared to majority of existing models)
● Developing a novel, compact characterization of biomass considering its
proximate analysis and structural components using machine learning
techniques
● Devising a multiphase statistical pathway needed as a precondition to
effectively quantify the entanglements of different important factors in the
process of biomass gasification in fluidized bed reactors

120
● Utilizing neural network computational framework to obtain numerical
values of the model’s weights and biases
● Separate results for bubbling and circulating, and then overall combined
gasifiers like the example presented in the following table 20.

6.1 Conclusions regarding the modeling approach
The no free lunch theorem states no machine learning algorithm is superior when
averaged over the same datasets.
An important question is what subset of collected data truly represent the
population under study. A neural network trained on that subset is likely to perform well
against completely new dataset. In other words, it is the material you study that
determines how you do on a test.
It appears that each observation is unique and that in every session of training
they show resistance to all the generalizing techniques although with various vigors.
It should be added that the training error can always be lowered (e.g with
increasing capacity of model) but it is the gap between training and test error that matters
the most. It was decided that the best combination is when this gap is minimum. The
most valuable configuration was achieved where the error on 70 previously unseen

121
datasets was slightly lower than the training error (13.78 vs 14.07). This particular NN
was trained using Bayesian algorithm, and sum of squared error was used as performance
metric. The 40 test datasets (from run 3 in Figure 72 (c) with error of 13.78) are listed in
the appendix D, it should be noted the remaining 30 datasets randomly selected within the
training algorithm are inaccessible.
6.2 Recommendations
One recommendation regarding the process is that it is certainly worth to
investigate dynamics of bubbling and circulating bed separately, same applies for
oxyfuel and air blown gasifiers. Also, if information available regarding other important
variables such as catalysts used in the bed, more details about the particles (i.e. density,
sphericity, …), steam temperature, temperature of air if there is pre heating and most
importantly the reactor geometry and size.
An important question arises that how successful the principle of triangle
inequality is in quantifying the non-equilibrium of a process, and what was the role of
centroid difference approach in predictivity of model.
“As of 2016 a rule of thumb is that a supervised deep learning algorithm will
generally achieve acceptable performance with around 5000 labeled examples per
category.” [52]
Working successfully with small datasets is an important research area in machine
learning. In that context, applying machine learning techniques to modeling physical
processes is limited by limitedness of experimental data specially for expensive
experiments such as gasification.

122
As far as the direction of research is concerned, additional improvements become
feasible by resolving the following issues and alike:
- “It is not clear now who at NETL really decides what multiphase research
area to follow.” [87]
- “The Multiphase Fluid Dynamics Research Consortium (MFDRC) was
established in 1998 in response to priority research needs identified in the
Vision 2020 Computational Fluid Dynamics Roadmap.” [87]
- “That initiative is a model that should be followed if there is ever going to be
an attempt to have a National Multiphase Computational Fluid Dynamics
Initiative.” [87]

the goal is to be leading candidate for:
***
Job
Faculty Position, TechnoEconomic Analysis/LCA for Energy & Climate Engineering Technologies (Open Rank)
The Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering invites applications for multiple faculty positions at the intersection of technoeconomic analysis (TEA), life cycle analysis (LCA), and emerging energy and climate engineering technologies (TEA/LCA Energy and Climate Engineering Technologies).
Position Description

The Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (PME) is a unique interdisciplinary school launched by the University of Chicago in 2011 with the aim of translating molecular and quantum science into technological solutions with potential societal impact in health and immunology, energy/water/materials, environmental sustainability, and quantum information technology. PME does groundbreaking research that spans polymeric materials, new water purification methods, battery materials, sensing applications, self-assembly of materials to prevent and treat disease, and more. PME is affiliated with Argonne National Laboratory, an independent unit within the university, and joint appointment is encouraged when appropriate.

The Climate Systems Engineering initiative was launched in 2023 as a university-wide initiative to apply insights from systems engineering and climate systems science to study technologies that might reduce the risks of accumulated greenhouse gases. It works to advance understanding of the potential benefits and risks of technologies including solar geoengineering from modification to surface albedo to space-based systems; open-systems carbon removal such as enhanced rock weathering and related methods of ocean carbon removal; and local interventions to reduce glacial melting. 

The Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering invites applications for multiple faculty positions (tenure-track assistant professor or tenured associate or full professor) at the intersection of technoeconomic analysis (TEA), life cycle analysis (LCA), and emerging energy and climate engineering technologies (TEA/LCA Energy and Climate Engineering Technologies). Tenure lines will be housed within the PME and successful candidates will be expected to affiliate with the UChicago Climate Systems Engineering Initiative (CSEi) https://climateengineering.uchicago.edu/.

Successful candidates’ primary research is expected to focus on conducting in-depth technoeconomic and life cycle analyses of emerging energy and climate engineering technologies. Ideal candidates will work closely with engineers, scientists, and business analysts to assess the environmental, economic, and technical feasibility of various energy and climate engineering technologies. The PME is a highly collaborative and interdisciplinary environment that promotes deep collaborative opportunities between modeling and experimental research groups.  

We welcome applicants working in developing models to simulate the economic impact of scaling technologies and comparing the economic performance of different technology pathways for decarbonization and climate engineering. Other areas of interest include (but are not limited to) assessing the environmental impacts associated with the entire lifecycle of energy and materials technologies; analysis of supply chain and material flows across stages of production, use, and end-of-life disposal or recycling; and quantifying greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, energy inputs, and other environmental impacts using software tools. We encourage collaboration with other PME and CSEi research teams to align analysis with technology development goals, particularly in emerging energy and climate engineering technologies, including but not limited to battery storage, carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS), carbon removal, hydrogen, and recycling or re-use technologies. We especially welcome applicants familiar with energy and carbon market analysis and integration of new technologies into existing systems, as well experience with energy, carbon, and climate policy analysis and regulatory frameworks.  

Qualifications

Before the start of employment, qualified applicants must hold a doctoral degree in a relevant field of study and have a strong record of independent research.  Candidates for Associate or Full Professor must have evidence of leadership in their field and an outstanding track record of independent research, allowing them to qualify for appointment as a tenured professor in the Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (or jointly with another department in the University). All successful candidates will be expected to establish and maintain a robust research program and teach at the graduate and undergraduate levels.

Application Instructions

Candidates should apply online through the University of Chicago’s Interfolio website: http://apply.interfolio.com/158546.

Applicants must upload:

Cover letter
CV including bibliography
Research statement (a statement describing past and current research accomplishments and outlining future research plans)
Teaching statement. This statement may also include the candidate’s experience in teaching diverse students. The University’s Diversity Statement can be found at https://provost.uchicago.edu/statements-diversity.
 Contact information for three references who can provide confidential letters of evaluation
 

The following materials are optional:

Up to three published or unpublished research papers
Review of applications will continue until the positions are filled. Please contact Daphne Gavins at ddgavins@uchicago.edu with any questions.

All University departments and institutes are charged with building a faculty from a diversity of backgrounds and with diverse viewpoints; with cultivating an inclusive community that values freedom of expression; and with welcoming and supporting all their members.

We seek a diverse pool of applicants who wish to join an academic community that places the highest value on rigorous inquiry and encourages diverse perspectives, experiences, groups of individuals, and ideas to inform and stimulate intellectual challenge, engagement, and exchange. The University’s Statements on Diversity are at https://provost.uchicago.edu/statements-diversity.

This position is benefits eligible – for information on benefits, please consult the University of Chicago Benefits Guide: https://mybenefits.nfp.com/UChicago/benefits-guide/.

The University of Chicago is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity/Disabled/Veterans Employer and does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, national or ethnic origin, age, status as an individual with a disability, military or veteran status, genetic information, or other protected classes under the law. For additional information please see the University’s Notice of Nondiscrimination.

Job seekers in need of a reasonable accommodation to complete the application process should call 773-834-3988 or email equalopportunity@uchicago.edu with their request.

BRUSSELS: Foreign Minister Adel Al-Jubeir gave a fitting reply to the consul general of Iran during a lecture at Egmont Research Center of the Foreign Ministry of Belgium in Brussels, after the consul alleged the Kingdom supported terrorism.

Al-Arabiya broadcast a part of the speech of the Iranian consul general, in which he said: “I believe that saying that Al-Qaeda has any relationship with Iran is a joke. Nobody has forgotten that Bin Laden was a Saudi national and he had strong political and economic relations with the Kingdom. They have also not forgotten that from among 19 people who participated in 9/11 attacks, 15 were Saudi nationals. People sitting in this hall also know which countries who have supported Daesh for several years are.”

Responding to this allegation, Al-Jubeir said: “I did not say anything which is not backed by facts. Doesn’t the Iranian constitution talk about exporting revolution? Doesn’t the Iranian constitution talk about taking care of deprived Shias? Didn’t Iran establish Hezbollah? Didn’t Iran attack more than 12 embassies inside Iran violating all international laws? We never attacked them. Iran did. Didn’t Iran engineer, plan and implement attacks on residences of the American forces in Alkhobar in 1996? Yes, they did.

The officer in charge of this operation was your military attaché in Bahrain. The person who made the bomb was from Hezbollah of Lebanon. The explosives came from Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley. The three main leaders of the operation ran away and has been living in Iran since then.”

Al-Jubeir continued: “When there were explosions in Riyadh in 2003, Saif Al-Adel was in Iran with Saad Bin Laden, Al-Qaed’s propaganda official, as well as another four or five commanders. We asked Iran to hand them over. But they refused our demand. Some of them are still in Iran.”

“The order for bombing the residential complexes of Riyadh in 2003 was given by Saif Al-Adel, commander of Al-Qaeda’s operations. He was then staying in Iran. We have recordings of telephone conversation. We did not create this information. Ronald Regan used to say: The facts are stubborn. They are actually stubborn because it is not possible to get around facts. Hezbollah is a terrorist organization. It is clear that it has attacked embassies. The embassies do not explode themselves. There must be somebody behind it. Diplomats do not kill themselves by firing bullets on themselves three times. There is a person responsible for this,” he added.

Al-Jubeir added: “Iranian agents have links with terrorist attacks in Europe and South America. We did not create these facts. This is the world and this is the proof. We wish that Iran would become a great neighbor. But this depends on both sides. If you want the world to deal with you, then there is a requirement of giving up hostile expansionist policies and return to international norms and practices.”

Addressing the Iranian consul directly, the foreign minister said: “If you don’t want Saudi officials criticizing Iran, then do not behave in a way which attracts criticism. So far your history is full of death and destruction, noncompliance with international law and the principles which have existed since the emergence of the United Nations, particularly those related to good neighborly relations and noninterference in the affairs of others.”

docs.content:
# Verifying IP3 Nuclear Lobbying Claims: Documentary Evidence Assessment

Both claims examined here are **substantially verified by primary source documents**—specifically emails, presentations, and communications obtained by the House Oversight Committee through its 2019 investigation. The Committee collected over 60,000 pages of documents from private companies, though the Trump White House refused to produce any documents, limiting the completeness of the record.

## The investigation and its documentary basis

The House Oversight and Reform Committee, under Chairman Elijah Cummings, conducted a major investigation into efforts to transfer sensitive U.S. nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia. Two interim staff reports were issued: a February 2019 report based on whistleblower testimony, and a more comprehensive **50-page July 2019 report** based on documentary evidence from IP3 International, Colony NorthStar (Thomas Barrack's company), and government agencies.

The underlying documents include internal IP3 emails, position papers sent to White House officials, PowerPoint presentations prepared for Jared Kushner, and text message records. The GOP minority issued a counter-report disputing the characterization of impropriety but did not dispute the documented contacts and lobbying activities themselves.

---

## Claim 1: IP3 lobbied against the Gold Standard

**ACCURACY SCORE: 92/100**

The claim states that IP3 pushed the Trump Administration not to require Saudi Arabia to agree to the "Gold Standard"—a commitment to forgo uranium enrichment and spent fuel reprocessing capabilities—complaining it would lock them out of lucrative contracts.

### Documentary evidence directly confirms this

Admiral Michael Hewitt, IP3's CEO, sent multiple emails and position papers opposing the Gold Standard to White House and Department of Energy officials:

- **April 23, 2017 email**: Hewitt wrote that "**Gold Standard has slowly killed our leverage**" and that "Insisting on a gold standard 123 agreement is banking on coercion vs cooperation as a strategy. Coercion alone is a losing strategy."

- **April 28-30, 2017**: Hewitt emailed White House officials Michael Catanzaro and George David Banks, then DOE officials Edward McGinnis and Suzanne Jaworowski, a formal IP3 position paper advocating against requiring Saudi Arabia to agree to the Gold Standard.

- **August 27, 2018**: Hewitt sent an NSC official a draft document arguing that "**continued USG insistence on the 'gold standard' will likely lock US companies forever out of the global market** for contracts in the nuclear industry."

Industry executives documented in the report described IP3 characterizing the Gold Standard as a "**total roadblock**" to their Middle East nuclear ambitions. Stuart Solomon, IP3's President, wrote in July 2018 that "the key folks know that a gold standard is not achievable."

### Minor accuracy deductions

The claim loses 8 points for two reasons. First, the phrase "currently pushing" in the claim is temporally imprecise—the documented lobbying occurred primarily in 2017-2018, not at the moment the claim was written. Second, while the documents clearly show IP3 urged abandoning the Gold Standard for commercial reasons, the White House's refusal to produce documents means we cannot fully verify whether this lobbying influenced actual policy decisions.

---

## Claim 2: Kushner meetings on Westinghouse acquisition

**ACCURACY SCORE: 95/100**

The claim states that IP3 officials met with Kushner, briefed him on their plan for Westinghouse to be acquired through foreign investments, and that Kushner expressed plans to convene senior-level interagency meetings.

### Kushner's own email confirms the meeting

On **August 2, 2017**, Kushner sent an email to IP3 advisor Dennis Ross after meeting with IP3 officials, stating: "Met them today and am trying to gather the interagency assessment of the importance, impact and national security considerations both domestically and internationally."

This single email directly confirms three elements of the claim: the meeting occurred, Kushner attended, and he committed to initiating an interagency process.

### IP3 prepared Westinghouse acquisition materials specifically for Kushner

A slide deck entitled **"IP3 Overview: Middle East Power Infrastructure and Security Initiative, Jared Kushner, August 2017"** documented the foreign investment plan. The presentation included a capitalization chart for acquiring Westinghouse showing a **30% "Foreign owned" equity stake** from a "Strategic Sovereign Fund" and foreign partner countries. One slide explicitly stated: "A Saudi strategic investment in Westinghouse would serve as a signal towards U.S. partnership."

### Follow-up communications corroborate interagency commitment

Two days after the meeting, Admiral Hewitt emailed Defense Department official Sally Donnelly summarizing that "Jared was going to engage Sec Tillerson on Weds and believe he plans to pull together a Deputies, Principals mtg to discuss national security, policy and domestic/international considerations of Middle East, Nuclear Power, Westinghouse and Russian movement to dominate the region/market."

### Minor accuracy deductions

The claim receives 95/100 because the evidence proving the meeting, the Westinghouse briefing, and Kushner's commitment to interagency meetings comes from Kushner's email and IP3's internal documents. The 5-point deduction reflects that the White House's complete non-cooperation means we cannot definitively verify whether the promised interagency meetings actually occurred afterward.

---

## Source credibility and limitations

The claims are based on the strongest available evidence category: **primary source documents obtained through congressional subpoena power**, including emails written by the principals themselves. The July 2019 report cites specific dates, participants, and direct quotes from internal communications.

Key credibility factors supporting these claims include multiple whistleblowers from within the NSC corroborating the documentary evidence, NSC Legal Advisor John Eisenberg ordering staff to stop working on IP3 matters due to conflicts of interest, and the contemporaneous nature of the documentary evidence (real-time emails, not after-the-fact accounts).

The primary limitation is that the Trump White House produced zero documents, meaning any communications that existed only within government systems remain unexamined. IP3 disputed some characterizations but did not dispute the authenticity of the cited documents. The Republican minority report challenged the interpretation of the evidence as "impropriety" but acknowledged the underlying contacts and lobbying occurred.

---

## Responses and subsequent developments

IP3 defended its activities as efforts to "empower the U.S. nuclear industry and counteract Russian and Chinese efforts" but declined to directly rebut the specific documented lobbying against the Gold Standard. Neither Kushner nor the White House responded substantively to the 2019 reports; spokespersons either declined comment or did not respond to media inquiries.

Thomas Barrack—IP3's key ally and Trump's inaugural chairman—was indicted in 2021 on charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent for the UAE. He was **acquitted of all charges** in November 2022. Notably, that prosecution concerned UAE lobbying, not the Saudi nuclear matters documented in the Oversight reports.

No criminal charges were ever filed specifically related to the IP3/Saudi nuclear lobbying or the Gold Standard advocacy. The congressional investigation was not completed before Chairman Cummings' death in October 2019 and was not continued when Republicans regained House control.

---

## Final accuracy assessment

| Claim | Score | Basis |
|-------|-------|-------|
| Claim 1: IP3 lobbied against Gold Standard | **92/100** | Multiple IP3 emails and position papers directly confirm lobbying White House/DOE officials against Gold Standard, citing concern about being locked out of contracts. Minor deductions for temporal imprecision and inability to verify policy impact. |
| Claim 2: Kushner met with IP3 on Westinghouse | **95/100** | Kushner's own email confirms meeting and interagency commitment. IP3 presentation for Kushner explicitly shows Westinghouse acquisition plan with foreign investment. Minor deduction only for uncertainty whether promised meetings occurred. |

Both claims are accurate representations of what the documentary evidence shows. The House Oversight Committee's findings were based on contemporaneous internal documents, not allegations or characterizations—the quoted language comes from the emails and presentations themselves.

# Jared Kushner and the proxy wealth pattern: A comparative analysis

The question of whether President Trump's son-in-law leveraged his White House position for subsequent financial gain follows documented patterns seen in autocratic regimes—though operating within America's more transparent legal framework. **Six months after leaving office, Kushner received $2 billion from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund despite its own advisors calling his operations "unsatisfactory in all aspects"**—a sequence that congressional investigators have characterized as raising "profound concerns about possible impropriety and quid pro quos."

The core parallel to documented international cases is unmistakable: a leader's relative holding a position shaping policy toward foreign states subsequently receives extraordinary financial benefits from those same states. What distinguishes the Kushner case is not the presence or absence of the pattern, but the degree of institutional transparency that allows such patterns to be documented and debated publicly.

## The Saudi investment defied internal risk assessment

On January 21, 2021—the day after Trump left office—Kushner incorporated Affinity Partners in Delaware. Six months later, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund committed **$2 billion**, representing approximately two-thirds of the firm's total assets. Internal PIF documents obtained by the New York Times reveal the fund's screening panel unanimously recommended against the investment, citing Kushner's complete lack of private equity experience, "unsatisfactory" operations, excessive proposed fees, and "public relations risks" arising from his government role.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally overruled these objections. The contrast with Steven Mnuchin's simultaneous investment is instructive: the former Treasury Secretary, with decades of financial experience, received half the amount on less favorable terms. By 2024, Affinity had collected **$157 million in management fees**—including **$87 million from Saudi Arabia alone**—while generating zero returns for investors.

The investment structure follows what ethics experts identify as a classic access-monetization model. Kushner collects approximately **$25 million annually** regardless of fund performance, plus 20% of any eventual profits. When the PIF asked why no U.S. institutional investors had committed capital, Affinity staff noted Kushner "would like to avoid media attention at this time." Today, **99% of Affinity's approximately $4.8 billion** comes from non-U.S. sources—overwhelmingly Gulf sovereign wealth funds.

## Kushner's White House tenure shaped Saudi-U.S. relations

The financial relationship cannot be separated from the policy relationship that preceded it. Kushner developed what multiple sources describe as an unusually close personal connection with MBS, communicating frequently via WhatsApp outside normal National Security Council protocols. According to reporting in The Intercept and elsewhere, MBS told associates that Kushner was "in his pocket."

Concrete policy outcomes favoring Saudi interests during Kushner's tenure include: arranging Trump's unprecedented first foreign trip to Riyadh in May 2017; personally negotiating a **$110 billion arms deal** subsequently featured in Affinity's investor pitch deck; supporting the Saudi-UAE blockade of Qatar over State Department objections; and pushing to share nuclear technology with Saudi Arabia despite warnings from senior national security officials that the effort was "unethical and potentially illegal."

Most consequentially, following the October 2018 murder and dismemberment of journalist Jamal Khashoggi by a Saudi team linked to MBS—after which the CIA concluded with "high confidence" that MBS personally ordered the killing—Kushner continued private communications with the crown prince and, according to Saudi sources, advised him on "how to weather the storm." By December 2018, Kushner publicly stated the administration's focus had "shifted away from the Khashoggi case." In February 2024, Kushner claimed he had not read the declassified intelligence report and called MBS a "visionary leader."

## The Qatar sequence raises the most direct conflict questions

The timeline connecting Kushner family financial distress to U.S. foreign policy toward Qatar represents the most documented potential conflict of interest. In 2007, at Jared Kushner's urging, Kushner Companies purchased 666 Fifth Avenue for **$1.8 billion**—the highest price ever paid for a New York office building. The deal, financed almost entirely with debt, became what Trump friend Tom Barrack called "the Jenga puzzle piece that could set the empire teetering." By 2017, with **$1.4 billion in debt** coming due in early 2019 and vacancy rates at 25-30%, the building threatened the family's financial survival.

The company sought rescue financing from multiple foreign sources. During the Trump transition, Kushner met with Qatari representatives at Trump Tower. In April 2017—three months into the administration—Charles Kushner met directly with **Qatar's Finance Minister** to request "just under a billion dollars." Qatar declined, citing "dubious business logic."

**Six weeks later**, the Saudi-UAE blockade of Qatar began. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, who was caught "by surprise" and called for easing the blockade due to humanitarian concerns and the U.S. military base in Qatar, found himself publicly contradicted by Trump within an hour. Tillerson later testified that Kushner "was more of a view that the blockading countries had good reason to do what they were doing." A Tillerson aide told author Vicky Ward that "the Saudis would not have risked moving forward without permission from somebody. That person must have been Jared." NBC reported that some Qatari officials believed "the White House's position on the blockade may have been a form of retaliation driven by Kushner who was sour about the failed deal."

In August 2018—after U.S. policy toward Qatar softened—Brookfield Asset Management finalized a **$1.28 billion deal** for a 99-year lease on 666 Fifth Avenue, paying the entire amount upfront. Brookfield publicly stated "no Qatar-linked entity has any involvement." However, Senator Ron Wyden's investigation documented that Qatar Investment Authority was **the second-largest investor** in Brookfield Property Partners, with approximately **$2 billion from Middle Eastern sources** comprising the relevant fund.

## Ethics machinery documented pervasive concerns

Career government officials repeatedly flagged Kushner's situation as problematic. White House whistleblower Tricia Newbold testified that Kushner had "significant disqualifying factors" including foreign influence, outside activities, and personal conduct. **Two career security specialists** recommended denying his top-secret clearance; President Trump personally ordered Chief of Staff John Kelly to grant it, with both Kelly and White House Counsel Don McGahn writing contemporaneous memos documenting their objections.

The Washington Post reported that officials in **four countries—UAE, China, Israel, and Mexico**—had discussed ways to manipulate Kushner through his business arrangements. The CIA "balked" at granting additional clearance access, with one officer calling to ask "how Kushner got even a top-secret clearance."

His financial disclosures required approximately **40 revisions**, with one amendment revealing **77 "inadvertently omitted" items** worth at least $10 million. Despite a December 2019 White House ethics determination that divesting from Cadre (a real estate platform he co-founded) was "reasonably necessary to avoid a conflict of interest," Kushner did not divest. Following meetings with Apollo Global Management's Joshua Harris, who was simultaneously advising the administration on infrastructure, Apollo facilitated a **$184 million loan** to Kushner family real estate holdings.

Congressional investigations produced limited accountability. House Oversight Chairwoman Carolyn Maloney's probe documented the Saudi investment concerns but stalled when Republicans gained control in 2023. Chairman James Comer acknowledged that Kushner "crossed the line of ethics" but declined to issue subpoenas, reportedly viewing investigation as "politically unsustainable." A Senate Intelligence Committee criminal referral to prosecutors over potential misleading testimony produced no known investigation.

## International proxy patterns show structural similarities

The documented cases of political relatives accumulating wealth through their positions—particularly in Kazakhstan and Tajikistan—reveal patterns that partially mirror the Kushner situation.

**Timur Kulibayev**, Kazakhstan's presidential son-in-law, built a **$10 billion fortune** while holding positions at state oil entities. ICIJ investigations documented his company receiving a **$1.06 billion no-bid contract** (later ballooning to $2.5 billion) from a Chevron-led consortium, with internal warnings about "improper payments to politically influential actors." His empire spans **220+ companies in 22 countries**, including 10 secrecy havens. Swiss authorities investigated approximately **$600 million** in allegedly fraudulent proceeds.

**Shamsullo Sohibov**, Tajikistan's presidential son-in-law, controls the Faroz conglomerate's **58+ businesses** spanning fuel, transport, banking, healthcare, and media. OCCRP documented land deals at steep discounts, regulatory capture (when Faroz invested in driving schools, the government shut down two-thirds of competitors), and the elimination of business rivals through criminal charges.

The mechanisms documented in these cases—offshore structures hiding beneficial owners, strategic industry access, preferential state treatment, timing of enrichment correlating with policy decisions—map onto Kushner's situation with important distinctions:

| Pattern | Kulibayev/Sohibov | Kushner |
|---------|-------------------|---------|
| Sovereign wealth investment | Not primary mechanism | $2B Saudi, $200M+ each Qatar/UAE |
| Strategic industry control | Direct (oil, banking, transport) | Indirect (investment advisory) |
| Government contracts | Documented no-bid awards | Allegations regarding 666 Fifth Ave |
| Offshore opacity | 220+ shell companies in secrecy havens | Structure limiting investor disclosure |
| Timing correlation | During tenure | Post-tenure (6 months after) |
| Institutional accountability | Investigations closed; critics arrested | Congressional scrutiny; no charges |

## Kushner maintains he followed all rules

Kushner has consistently defended his conduct. At an Axios summit in 2022, he stated: "I followed every law and ethics rule" and challenged critics: "Point to a single decision we made that wasn't in [America's interest]." His spokesperson told the New York Times that "Mr. Kushner fully abided by all legal and ethical guidelines both during and after his government service."

On the Saudi investment specifically, Kushner has noted that PIF holds stakes in Microsoft, Uber, and Nintendo—positioning himself as one of many legitimate recipients of Gulf capital. His memoir *Breaking History* frames his Middle East work as advancing genuine diplomatic goals, and supporters credit him with the Abraham Accords normalizing relations between Israel and several Arab states.

Brookfield explicitly denied any "quid pro quo" in the 666 Fifth Avenue transaction. Charles Kushner claimed he "purposefully avoided doing business with sovereign investment funds to avoid a conflict of interest"—though this contradicts documented April 2017 meetings with Qatari officials and the subsequent Brookfield structure involving Qatari capital.

Ethics experts remain skeptical. Kathleen Clark of Washington University called it "a swamp monster" situation where Kushner "exploit[ed] his access to the president" for "extraordinary personal financial benefit." Steve Rattner noted the unprecedented concentration: "I have never seen someone get $2 billion out of $3 billion, two-thirds of their money, from a single investor."

## The pattern comparison reveals both parallels and distinctions

Jared Kushner's situation exhibits several hallmarks of the documented proxy wealth accumulation pattern: a relative positioned to influence policy toward foreign governments; subsequent financial benefits from those governments; timing that suggests quid pro quo relationships; structures limiting transparency; and professional defenders offering plausible deniability.

The **critical similarities** include: sovereign wealth fund investment despite advisor objections; policy advocacy benefiting the investing country; timing correlations between policy decisions and financial benefits; use of structures (private equity fund exemptions) to limit disclosure requirements; and family business rescue potentially connected to foreign government interests.

The **critical differences** include: operating within a system of institutional checks, congressional oversight, and press freedom that makes such patterns publicly documentable; facing ethics requirements and disclosure obligations that, however poorly enforced, create a record; and concentrating questionable benefits primarily in the post-government period rather than during active service.

Whether this constitutes illegal conduct remains unresolved. Congressional investigators characterized the pattern as raising "profound concerns about possible impropriety and quid pro quos." Senator Wyden's October 2024 request for a special counsel to investigate potential Foreign Agents Registration Act violations remains pending. What is documented is that Kushner's post-government wealth accumulation—**rising 180% to at least $900 million** according to Forbes—flowed predominantly from governments whose interests he advanced while in office.

The comparison to Kazakhstan and Tajikistan ultimately illuminates not identical conduct but a spectrum. Authoritarian regimes permit relatives to capture state assets directly and prosecute those who document it. The American system generates transparency that enables debate while producing limited accountability. Kushner operated closer to ethical boundaries than precedent suggested acceptable for senior government officials—collecting **tens of millions annually** from the government of a crown prince he defended after a journalist's murder—yet faces no legal consequences beyond unfavorable congressional reports and investigative journalism.

## Conclusion

The documented record supports the conclusion that Jared Kushner's situation exhibits structural parallels to international cases of political relatives used as wealth accumulation proxies—while operating within constraints that distinguish democratic from authoritarian systems. The $2 billion Saudi investment, occurring six months after Kushner left an office where he shaped Saudi policy, over the objections of the fund's own risk advisors, generates ongoing fees regardless of investment performance. The Qatar sequence—financing request, rejection, blockade support, eventual bailout through Qatar-linked capital—follows a pattern that investigators found warranted scrutiny even if it cannot be definitively characterized as corrupt.

What the comparison reveals is less about individual culpability than institutional failure. The ethics infrastructure designed to prevent conflicts of interest—disclosure requirements, recusal obligations, security clearance processes—was systematically overridden when it produced inconvenient conclusions. The result is a documented case of what ethics professor Kathleen Clark called "translat[ing] access to the president and power within the administration directly into personal financial benefit"—the core definition of the proxy wealth pattern, operating within American institutional constraints that document rather than prevent the behavior.

docs.content:
# Working Capital Survivability Thresholds for Small Businesses

**The median U.S. small business holds only 27 days of cash reserves**—barely enough to survive a single month-long disruption—while 82% of business failures trace directly to cash flow mismanagement. This critical gap between recommended reserves (3-6 months) and actual holdings creates a persistent vulnerability that recent inflation, rising interest rates, and tightening credit have dramatically amplified. Business bankruptcy filings surged **40.3% in 2024**, with small business Chapter V elections increasing 61%, signaling an accelerating cash crisis across the sector.

---

## The 27-day vulnerability defines small business survival

JPMorgan Chase Institute's landmark analysis of 597,000 businesses reveals stark reality: the typical small business operates with a **27-day cash buffer**—the number of days current cash balances could cover average daily outflows. More alarming, **25% of small businesses hold fewer than 13 days** of cash reserves, placing them in immediate danger from any revenue disruption.

Cash vulnerability varies dramatically by industry. Restaurants operate on the thinnest margins at just **16 median cash buffer days**, while real estate firms enjoy relative security with **47 days**. This pattern follows predictable lines: labor-intensive businesses average only 23 days versus 38 days for capital-intensive operations, and low-wage industries hold 19 days versus 31 days in high-wage sectors.

| Industry | Median Cash Buffer Days | Risk Level |
|----------|------------------------|------------|
| Restaurants | 16 | Critical |
| Repair & Maintenance | 18 | High |
| Retail | 19 | High |
| Construction | 20 | High |
| **All Small Businesses** | **27** | Moderate |
| High-Tech Services | 33 | Lower |
| Real Estate | 47 | Lower |

The consequences of thin reserves are severe. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports **20.4% of businesses fail within year one**, rising to 48.4% by year five and 65.1% by year ten. Yet these aggregate statistics obscure the dominant pattern: **82% of failures stem from cash flow problems**, according to U.S. Bank research—making working capital the single most predictive factor in business survival.

---

## Micro and small businesses face disproportionate capital constraints

Business scale fundamentally shapes working capital dynamics, with smaller firms facing compounding disadvantages in reserves, access to credit, and ability to absorb shocks.

**Micro businesses (1-9 employees)** operate with the thinnest margins. Personal services firms hold a median daily cash balance of just **$5,300**, while restaurants average $5,900. These businesses rely heavily on owner financing—**87% depend on the owner's personal credit score** for funding access. The Federal Reserve's Small Business Credit Survey shows 77% of micro-business loan applications at large banks face rejection.

**Small businesses (10-49 employees)** transition into more formalized financial management but still struggle. Working capital needs scale with payroll obligations, yet access to credit lines remains constrained. Average small business loan amounts through online marketplaces hover around **$38,000**, insufficient for sustained operations during downturns.

**Medium businesses (50-249 employees)** achieve greater stability through scale economies, improved supplier bargaining power, and broader financing options. SBA 7(a) loans average **$443,097**, while 504 loans average **$1.1 million**, providing meaningful runway for established operations.

Revenue-based analysis reveals similar patterns. Businesses under $1 million in annual revenue face the highest failure rates and most limited financing options. The Kauffman Foundation finds average startup capital of just **$78,000**—though firms with strong credit average $136,000, and high-tech ventures reach $275,000. Critically, **83% of entrepreneurs never access bank loans or venture capital**, relying instead on personal and family savings (65%) and credit cards (10%).

---

## Geographic disparities create working capital variations of 200-300%

Working capital requirements swing dramatically across states, driven by commercial rents, labor costs, tax burdens, and regulatory environments. A business requiring $50,000 monthly working capital in Mississippi might need $100,000-$150,000 for equivalent operations in New York.

**Commercial rent** represents the most variable cost factor. New York commands **$38.92 per square foot** annually, while Kansas averages just $17.32 for retail space. Los Angeles retail reaches $361.25 per square foot in premium locations. Bank of America Institute data shows rent's share of total business expenses jumped from **5.9% in 2019 to 9.1% in 2024**—with Las Vegas businesses paying more than double the national average.

**State tax climates** create structural advantages for cash preservation. The Tax Foundation's 2024 rankings identify Wyoming, South Dakota, and Alaska as most favorable for business (no corporate or individual income taxes), while New Jersey ranks worst with the nation's highest property, corporate, and individual rates. Massachusetts fell 12 places in rankings after implementing a surtax.

| State Category | Representative States | Key Characteristics |
|----------------|----------------------|---------------------|
| **Lowest WC Requirements** | Wyoming, South Dakota, Mississippi | No income taxes, $50-150 LLC fees, low rent |
| **Moderate WC Requirements** | Texas, Ohio, Indiana | Balanced costs, business-friendly regulation |
| **Highest WC Requirements** | New York, California, Massachusetts | $38+ sqft rent, $15+ minimum wage, high taxes |

Urban-rural differences add another dimension. While rural businesses have higher credit approval rates (59% vs. 50% urban), they show slower growth—small rural business employment grew only **1% from 2012-2019** compared to 12.9% for large rural firms. Regional Federal Reserve data reveals metro cash buffer days range from just **11 days in Atlanta and Orlando to 18 days in San Francisco**—a 60% variance.

---

## Cash infusions follow predictable patterns but access remains unequal

The anatomy of small business capital injections reveals critical thresholds for survival and stark disparities in access across demographic groups.

**Typical infusion amounts** cluster around specific thresholds by business type:
- **Startups**: Average $78,000 initial capital (Kauffman Foundation)
- **Operating businesses**: 40% of applicants seek less than $50,000
- **SBA 7(a) recipients**: Average $443,097 (FY 2024)
- **SBA 504 recipients**: Average $1.1 million

**Timing requirements** follow the 30/90/180 framework. Businesses with fewer than **30 days of runway** enter the critical danger zone requiring immediate action. Those with **90 days** have moderate flexibility for adjustment, while **180+ days** provides genuine stability. Industry consensus recommends 12-18 months between funding rounds, though actual gaps average 22 months according to Crunchbase.

**Sources of working capital** reveal heavy reliance on personal resources:
- **63.3%** use personal funds exclusively
- **65%** tap personal/family savings
- **39%** apply to large banks (down from 44% in 2023)
- Small banks deliver highest approval rates at **54%**

Access disparities remain stark. Black-owned businesses receive only **1.5% of outside equity** compared to 17% for white-owned firms, with loan approvals three times less likely. Women-owned businesses see 45% full approval versus 55% for men. New Black-owned businesses launch with nearly **three times less total capital** than white-owned counterparts.

---

## Critical financial ratios define the survival boundary

Empirical research identifies specific ratio thresholds that separate surviving businesses from those heading toward failure.

**Current ratio** (current assets divided by current liabilities) provides the primary liquidity signal:
- **Below 1.0**: Danger zone—liabilities exceed assets
- **1.0-1.2**: Warning territory
- **1.2-2.0**: Healthy range for most industries
- **Above 2.0**: May indicate inefficient capital deployment

Industry context matters significantly. Biotechnology firms average 5.15 (high R&D cash needs), while airlines operate at 0.57 (stable cash flows from advance bookings). The "sweet spot" of 1.0-1.5 represents optimal efficiency for most sectors.

**Quick ratio** (excluding inventory) offers a stricter test:
- **Below 0.5**: Severe distress
- **0.5-1.0**: Acceptable for inventory-heavy retail
- **1.0-2.0**: Strong liquidity position

**Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)** benchmarks vary by sector:
| Industry | DSO (Days) |
|----------|-----------|
| Engineering & Construction | 100 |
| Consulting | 78-90 |
| Technology | 55-65 |
| Healthcare | 45-60 |
| Retail | 10-15 |

The **Cash Conversion Cycle** (CCC) measures efficiency of working capital. Targets of under 30 days indicate optimal performance, while cycles exceeding 60 days signal working capital stress. Pharmaceutical companies average 128 days due to long inventory cycles, while grocery retailers achieve 9-15 days through rapid turnover.

**Altman Z-Score** thresholds predict bankruptcy probability:
- **Above 2.675**: Safe zone
- **1.8-2.675**: Gray zone requiring attention
- **Below 1.8**: High bankruptcy probability

---

## The 2023-2025 environment has intensified working capital pressures

Recent economic conditions have transformed small business capital requirements from challenging to critical, with multiple pressures compounding simultaneously.

**Bankruptcy filings** signal accelerating distress. Total U.S. bankruptcy filings reached **517,308 in 2024**, up 14.2% from 2023. Business bankruptcies surged 40.3% to 22,060 filings. Small business Subchapter V elections increased **61%** from 730 to 1,176 in the first half of 2024 alone.

**Inflation's impact** on working capital has been severe:
- **75% of firms** cite rising costs as their primary challenge (Fed SBCS 2024)
- **88%** of owners report inflation impacts
- **45%** have foregone their own paychecks due to cash flow shortages
- Construction equipment prices rose **nearly 25%** from January 2020 to March 2023
- Average wages increased 4% from July 2023 to July 2024

**Interest rates** have elevated borrowing costs substantially:
- Average small business term loans: **7.31-7.61%** (Q4 2024)
- SBA loans: **13.50%** average APR
- Credit standards have tightened for **13 consecutive quarters**
- More than half of small businesses cannot afford loans at current rates

**EIDL debt burden** continues weighing on survivors:
- **$380 billion** disbursed to 4 million businesses
- **$300+ billion** remains outstanding
- **67%** of firms with EIDL debt have over $100,000 total debt
- **52%** report challenges making payments
- SBA has charged off **$78.8 billion** through March 2024

The Federal Reserve's 2024 survey captures the cumulative effect: **56% of firms struggle to pay operating expenses**, **51% face uneven cash flows**, and denial rates for "too much existing debt" jumped from 22% in 2021 to **41% in 2024**.

---

## Conclusion: Survival requires meeting defined thresholds

Small business survivability centers on maintaining working capital above specific, empirically-validated thresholds that vary by size, industry, and geography. The critical findings converge on clear recommendations:

**Minimum cash reserves** should target 3-6 months of operating expenses—yet 70% of businesses hold less than four months and 39% have less than one month. Closing this gap represents the single highest-impact intervention for survival.

**Ratio thresholds** that define the survival boundary include current ratios above 1.2, quick ratios above 1.0, and DSO under 45 days. Businesses consistently operating below these levels face elevated failure risk regardless of profitability.

**Geographic selection** materially impacts requirements, with working capital needs varying 2-3x between lowest-cost states (Wyoming, Mississippi) and highest-cost markets (New York, California). This variation increasingly influences business formation and survival patterns.

**Access to timely capital** remains the decisive factor. The 82% failure rate attributable to cash flow reflects not just inadequate reserves but inability to secure infusions when needed. Small banks' 54% approval rate versus large banks' lower rates suggests relationship banking remains critical for survival-stage financing.

The 2023-2025 environment has raised effective thresholds across all metrics. Businesses that survived pre-pandemic with 30-day reserves now require 60-90 days; those that operated at 1.2 current ratios may need 1.5+. Inflation, interest rates, and accumulated EIDL debt have created a new baseline—and the 40% surge in business bankruptcies confirms that many enterprises have fallen below it.

By [Dr. Mohsen Dirbaz]
Preface

subsequent generations through path dependency mechanisms. Applied to America, this framework
explains patterns that other theories cannot: why the wealthiest democracy exhibits the highest out-of-
wedlock birth rates among peer nations, why educational capacity collapses despite abundant
resources, why fiscal stability erodes despite economic strength, why wellness outcomes lag despite
medical technology, and why massive institutional wealth coincides with worsening social outcomes.
The central analytical tool—the void fraction methodology—adapts concepts from materials science to
quantify institutional absence. In physics, void fraction measures the proportion of space that is empty
rather than solid. Applied to social systems, it measures the gap between institutional necessity and
institutional presence. The United States exhibits a 40.5% commitment void (births outside marriage), an
educational void of approximately 400,000 missing teachers, an 18.3% decline in fiscal reserve status, a
106% higher disability rate than peer nations, and near-total stewardship voids in religious institutions
controlling $1.2-4.8 trillion in assets while social outcomes deteriorate.
These voids are not independent but interconnected, forming a network of structural absence that
compounds across generations. The framework reveals American exceptionalism not as virtue but as

pathology—clustered dysfunctions traceable to founding composition through identifiable transmission
mechanisms.
The argument proceeds systematically. Chapter 1 establishes historical demographics, develops the
genealogical inheritance hypothesis within path dependency theory, and introduces the void fraction
measurement framework. Chapters 2-3 quantify commitment voids through detailed demographic
analysis and international comparison. Chapter 4 examines institutional voids in education, stewardship,
and accountability. Chapter 5 analyzes transmission mechanisms and addresses why conventional
interventions fail and finishes with a common sense proposal in epilogue.
This is not an anti-American polemic but an empirical analysis. The data come from official government
statistics, peer-reviewed research, and international organizations. The theoretical framework draws on
established work in historical institutionalism, cultural transmission, and comparative political economy.
The policy implications are pragmatic rather than ideological.
The skeleton in America’s closet is not what the nation did but what it is: a social structure defined by
absence, inheriting voids from populations who fled the very institutions and commitments now lacking.
Whether Americans can confront this reality and construct countervailing institutions remains uncertain.
But confronting it is the necessary first step toward any genuine transformation.
The void expands. The structure weakens. This book quantifies the absence and traces its origins. What
Americans choose to do with that knowledge will determine whether the nation can fill its voids or
whether it will collapse into them.
